title: How do you implement concurrency control for the "last item / last ticket" problem as a progression: `synchronized`/`ReentrantLock`/`AtomicInteger`/`ConcurrentHashMap` (single JVM only) → DB optimistic/pessimistic locking → Redis distributed lock (`SETNX` + TTL) across many instances → a queue that serializes requests to one consumer (no locks needed)?
shortTitle: How do you implement concurrency control for the "last item / last ticket" problem as a progression
keyPoints: The last-item problem is a check-then-act race: many requests see stock=1, all decrement, and you oversell.
Rung 1: In-JVM primitives (synchronized, AtomicInteger CAS) work only within one process.
Rung 2: DB locking (optimistic version column or pessimistic SELECT FOR UPDATE) works across instances sharing one DB.
Rung 3: Redis distributed lock (SET NX PX ttl) works across instances without a shared lockable row.
Rung 4: A single-consumer queue serializes requests so no lock is needed and no contention exists.
Use the cheapest technique whose scope matches your deployment; climb only when scaling out breaks the previous rung.
Prefer a database constraint over a Redis lock whenever the resource is a row you can constrain.

s1_definition.oneliner: For the last unit, use in-JVM locks within one process, database locking across instances sharing a DB, a Redis SETNX lock across instances without a shared row, or a single-consumer queue that serializes requests so no lock is needed.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **Check-then-act race** – Multiple threads read stock=1, all decide to take it, all decrement, causing overselling.
- **In-JVM primitives** – `synchronized`, `ReentrantLock`, `AtomicInteger.compareAndSet`; work only within one JVM.
- **DB optimistic locking** – Version column guarded UPDATE; retry on conflict; good for rare contention.
- **DB pessimistic locking** – `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE` blocks other transactions; good for high contention.
- **Redis distributed lock** – `SET key NX PX ttl` ensures only one caller wins across distributed instances.
- **Single-consumer queue** – All requests funnel through one consumer; eliminates contention by serialization.
s1_definition.analogy: National Bank of India is giving away one last festival gift voucher and a hundred customers reach for it at once. If one counter, the teller uses one hand. If many counters share one ledger, each teller checks and marks carefully. If counters do not share a ledger, they agree on a talking stick. Or the bank forms one line to one teller.

sections.s3_flow:
```text
  Concurrency Control Progression:

  Rung 1: In-JVM (single instance)
  ┌────────────────────────────┐
  │ AtomicInteger stock = 1    │
  │ Thread A: CAS(1,0) = true  │ GOT IT
  │ Thread B: CAS(1,0) = false │ SOLD OUT
  └────────────────────────────┘

  Rung 2: DB Locking (multi-instance)
  ┌────────┐  ┌────────┐  ┌────────────────┐
  │ Inst-1 │  │ Inst-2 │  │    Database     │
  │ UPDATE │──┤ UPDATE │──┤ WHERE qty > 0   │
  │ 1 row  │  │ 0 rows │  │ (atomic guard)  │
  └────────┘  └────────┘  └────────────────┘

  Rung 3: Redis Lock (no shared row)
  ┌────────┐  ┌────────┐  ┌────────────────┐
  │ Inst-1 │  │ Inst-2 │  │    Redis       │
  │ SET NX │──┤ SET NX │──┤ NX: first wins │
  │ true   │  │ false  │  │ PX: TTL 10s    │
  └────────┘  └────────┘  └────────────────┘

  Rung 4: Queue (zero contention)
  ┌────────┐  ┌────────┐  ┌───────┐  ┌──────────┐
  │ Inst-1 │──│ Inst-2 │──│ Queue │──│ Consumer │
  │ publish│  │ publish│  │       │  │ (single) │
  └────────┘  └────────┘  └───────┘  └──────────┘
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
The last-item problem is a check-then-act race: many concurrent requests read stock=1, all decide to buy, and all decrement, causing overselling. Every technique in the progression makes the check-and-decrement atomic at a particular scope, and you climb one rung at a time as deployment grows.

In-JVM primitives like AtomicInteger.compareAndSet work within one process. Database locking with a conditional UPDATE works across instances sharing one database. A Redis distributed lock with SET NX PX works when there is no lockable database row. A single-consumer queue removes contention entirely by serializing all requests.

At National Bank of India, Pankaj walked this progression. A single-instance service sold the last fixed-deposit slot twice, so he used AtomicInteger CAS. When they scaled out, that broke because each instance had its own counter, so he moved to a conditional UPDATE. For a one-time festival coupon not in the database, he used a Redis lock. And during a flash sale when even database locks thrashed, he serialized claims through a Kafka queue.

Remember one sentence: use the cheapest concurrency technique whose scope matches your deployment: AtomicInteger CAS within one JVM, conditional DB UPDATE across instances, Redis SET NX for non-DB resources, or a single-consumer queue for extreme contention.
